little.say: This is your heart. Thump, thump! It pumps your blood.

young.what: Your heart is a strong muscle in your chest, about the size of your fist.
young.does: It squeezes again and again to push blood all around your body.
young.funFact: Your heart beats about 100,000 times every day!

junior.what: The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers, found in the chest between the lungs.
junior.does: The right side pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body. Valves inside keep the blood flowing one way.
junior.funFact: The 'lub-dub' sound of your heartbeat is made by the heart's valves closing.
junior.details: The heart is made of a special muscle called cardiac muscle, built to keep working your whole life.

bipc.definition: The heart is a hollow, muscular, four-chambered organ of mesodermal origin that pumps blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulations.
bipc.structure: It lies in the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, and is protected by a double-walled pericardium enclosing pericardial fluid. It has two relatively small upper atria and two larger, thick-walled lower ventricles, separated by the interatrial and interventricular septa. The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening and the bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left; semilunar valves guard the openings into the pulmonary artery and aorta. Specialised nodal tissue includes the sino-atrial (SA) node, atrio-ventricular (AV) node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.
bipc.function: The SA node generates the maximum number of action potentials (about 70–75 per minute) and therefore acts as the pacemaker. One cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 s and consists of atrial systole, ventricular systole and joint diastole. Each ventricle pumps out about 70 mL of blood per beat (stroke volume), giving a cardiac output of about 5 L per minute. Double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

keyTerms.meaning: Pacemaker of the heart, in the upper right corner of the right atrium
Volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per beat (about 70 mL)
Volume pumped by each ventricle per minute = stroke volume × heart rate
Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: pulmonary and systemic

physicsLinks.explanation: For a steady flow, the volume passing per second is constant, so flow is slowest where the total cross-sectional area is largest. That is why blood moves most slowly through the capillaries, giving time for exchange.

commonMistakes: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood, the reverse of most arteries and veins.
examTips: Cardiac output ≈ 70 mL × 72 beats per minute ≈ 5 L per minute.

How long is one cardiac cycle at 72 beats per minute?

young.what: The aorta is the biggest blood tube in your body.
young.does: It carries bright red, oxygen-rich blood from your heart to the rest of your body.
young.funFact: Your aorta is about as wide as a garden hose!

junior.what: The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It leaves the left ventricle of the heart.
junior.does: It arches over the heart and runs down through the chest and abdomen, branching into arteries that supply the whole body with oxygen-rich blood.
junior.funFact: The aorta's elastic walls stretch with each heartbeat and spring back, which keeps blood flowing between beats.
junior.details: It has three main parts: the ascending aorta, the arch of the aorta and the descending aorta.

junior.what: The venae cavae are the two largest veins: the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava.
junior.does: They bring oxygen-poor blood from the upper and lower body back into the right atrium of the heart.
junior.funFact: The inferior vena cava is the widest vein in the body.
junior.details: Blood in veins is under low pressure, so veins have thinner walls than arteries.

young.what: Arteries are tubes that carry blood away from your heart.
young.does: They take oxygen and food from your blood to every part of your body.
young.funFact: You can feel blood pushing through an artery in your wrist. That's your pulse!

junior.what: Arteries are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart.
junior.does: Their thick, muscular and elastic walls cope with the high pressure of each heartbeat. Arteries branch into smaller arterioles and then into tiny capillaries.
junior.funFact: Your pulse is the stretch of an artery wall each time your heart beats.
junior.details: Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood. The pulmonary arteries are the exception: they carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

young.what: Veins are tubes that carry blood back to your heart.
young.does: They bring blood back so it can be sent to your lungs to pick up fresh oxygen.
young.funFact: Veins can look blue through your skin, but the blood inside is dark red!

junior.what: Veins are blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart.
junior.does: They have thinner walls than arteries, and many contain valves that stop blood from flowing backwards.
junior.funFact: Muscles squeezing around the veins, especially in your legs, help push blood back up to your heart.
junior.details: In diagrams, veins are coloured blue and arteries red, but all blood is actually red.

junior.what: The pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins connect the heart with the lungs.
junior.does: Pulmonary arteries (blue in the model) carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Pulmonary veins (red) bring oxygen-rich blood back to the left atrium.
junior.funFact: After birth, they are the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood and the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood.
junior.details: This short loop from the heart to the lungs and back is called the pulmonary circulation.

junior.what: The coronary arteries are small arteries that run over the surface of the heart.
junior.does: They carry oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle itself, which needs its own supply to keep pumping.
junior.funFact: 'Coronary' comes from the Latin word for crown, because these arteries circle the heart like a crown.
junior.details: They branch off the aorta just above the heart. If one becomes blocked, part of the heart muscle cannot get enough oxygen.
